metadata.title: About | Alessio Quagliara
metadata.description: Who I am: someone who ran a software house, now studying Computer Engineering and building micro-SaaS, web apps and automations without much ceremony.

hero.title: I build software and micro-SaaS made to last
hero.intro: I'm Alessio. I study Computer Engineering (Intelligent Systems), I started a software house and closed it. Now I build micro-SaaS products, web apps and automations for agencies, freelancers and SMEs. Few promises, code that holds up.

principles.title: Four rules. I learned them the hard way.

items.title: Architectural pragmatism
items.text: The simplest solution that holds. No microservices for a contact form: I've done my time with overengineering.

items.title: Build in Public
items.text: Projects, numbers and mistakes go on the blog. Even the ones that make me look bad.

items.title: Software & real-world IoT
items.text: When the data starts outside the screen, I go lower: C, ESP32, sensors.

items.title: Long-term maintainability
items.text: Code you can still read in two years, even if someone else opens it. Fewer parts, fewer surprises.

steps.title: My first e-commerce, never launched
steps.text: Car parts, a 14-day Shopify trial and no launch. First lesson: an idea isn't enough.

steps.title: Lyara and dropshipping
steps.text: Shopify, ads, copy, content. I lost money and gained a trade.

steps.title: Be Social
steps.text: My first web agency. Clients yes, margins no. That's when I moved everything to development.

steps.title: Spotex SRL
steps.text: A software house founded with partners, then closed. I learned more there than in any course.

steps.title: LinkBay-CMS
steps.text: Born as a platform for agencies, trademark filed in 2025. Now I'm cutting it down to what matters: an SEO tool for decaying content.

steps.title: RStudy and PivotCut
steps.text: An app to study without the chaos and a macOS app for 2D animation, heading to its first release on itch.io. Built in public.

steps.title: Automation technician
steps.text: PLCs, electronics, networks. That's where I learned software sooner or later touches something physical.

steps.title: Arduino and ESP32
steps.text: Prototypes on a cutting mat: sensors, lean firmware, data sent to a backend.

steps.title: n8n and Node-RED
steps.text: Flows that connect tools, CRMs and APIs. If you do a step by hand every week, it's a candidate.

steps.title: Back to C
steps.text: To understand what happens underneath: memory, I/O, performance. I write about it on the blog.

steps.title: Local AI
steps.text: Local models with Ollama and llama.cpp, for people who don't want their data leaving the building.

useCases.title: Three workflows that almost always get automated

items.label: Onboarding
items.problem: Contract signed, then: Drive folder, access, welcome email, tasks in the project manager. By hand every time, and something gets missed.
items.solution: The signature or payment kicks everything off: folder, access, email and tasks get created on their own, the same way every time.
items.result: The client starts the same day. Nobody has to remember the checklist.

items.label: Lead Management
items.problem: Leads from forms, email and DMs. They reach the CRM when someone remembers. Some never get a reply.
items.solution: Every lead lands in the CRM on its own, with source and priority. AI drafts a reply, you approve it.
items.result: No lost leads, first reply the same day.

items.label: Automated reports
items.problem: End of month: export from Analytics, Ads and sheets, paste into slides, format. For every client.
items.solution: Data collects itself into one report format for everyone. You only add the commentary.
items.result: The report is ready on the 1st. You write two lines and send it.

useCases.title: Three bottlenecks I see a lot

items.label: Orders from PDFs
items.problem: Customer orders arrive as PDFs, each in its own format. Someone retypes them into the system, line by line.
items.solution: AI reads the PDF (with OCR where needed), extracts codes, quantities and dates and checks them against master data and price lists. A person approves before import.
items.result: Entry time per order and typos, before and after. Data goes in once, already checked.

items.label: Machine data
items.problem: Parts made and downtime get logged at the end of the day, from memory or on paper. The data arrives late and dirty.
items.solution: An ESP32 with sensors reads part counts and machine state and sends them to a small backend. The PLC stays untouched unless it's needed.
items.result: Parts and downtime in real time, measured instead of guessed. After two weeks, compare against the handwritten log.

items.label: Job tracking
items.problem: A job's status lives in Excel, in chat and in someone's head. To know where it stands, you call around.
items.solution: A small web tool: each department updates the status with a tap, from PC, tablet or QR. The office sees everything on one page.
items.result: Status calls and late-discovered delays, counted before and after.

items.title: We don't touch what works
items.text: I work next to the ERP and software you already have: I connect, I don't replace. No system change, no downtime.

items.title: Pilot prototype in 7–10 days
items.text: One workflow, wired to real data. Validated on the floor before spending at scale.

items.title: Zero lock-in
items.text: Clean, documented code on your server or cloud. If you switch supplier tomorrow, you don't start over.

finalCta.title: 30 minutes to find out whether your bottleneck can be automated.
finalCta.text: Technical audit or exploratory call: we look at a real workflow, I tell you what I'd do and how long it'd take. If it isn't worth it, I'll say so.

items.question: Do we need to replace our ERP, management software or MES?
items.answer: No. I work next to them: connecting, collecting data, adding what's missing.

items.question: Can we start with a single process?
items.answer: Yes, that's the right way. One workflow, one result you can check.

items.question: Is AI required?
items.answer: No. Integrations, rules and alerts are often enough.

items.question: How do you handle data and access?
items.answer: Only the access needed, agreed in writing and documented. We decide together which data can leave. Any compliance requirements are checked with you before we start.

items.question: What does the free pilot include?
items.answer: {slots} spots until {deadline}. Mapping one workflow, a proposed change and, if it makes sense, a first integration. It's not a full project for free. In return I share the journey as a case study, only with what you approve.

items.question: How long does a first test take?
items.answer: A pilot prototype in 7–10 days from mapping, as long as access is in place. Validate first, then decide whether to scale.

items.question: What happens after the pilot?
items.answer: You decide: extend with a clear quote, adjust, or stop. No commitment.
